# Introduction to APIs and How Apps Talk to Each Other

##### Why your automation tool is really just a very polite phone caller

When you build a Zap that posts a Slack message, Zapier is not doing anything magical. It is making a phone call — a very structured, machine-readable phone call — to a computer at Slack, saying: *"Hello, here is proof of who I am, please put this text in channel #sales."* Slack's computer answers: *"Done, here is the message ID."*

That conversation happens over an **API**: an Application Programming Interface, the agreed-upon set of requests one piece of software will accept from another. Every no-code automation platform on earth is, underneath the friendly drag-and-drop surface, an API client with good manners.

This is the single most leverage-dense day of your first two weeks. Once you understand APIs, three things become true: you can use *any* app in *any* automation tool (including apps with no pre-built integration, via a generic HTTP step), you can debug failures instead of guessing, and you can read documentation instead of hunting for a YouTube tutorial that may not exist.

##### The restaurant menu analogy — and where it breaks

The classic explanation: an API is like a restaurant menu. It tells you exactly what you can order and how to ask. You do not walk into the kitchen and cook; you place a structured order and food arrives.

It is a good analogy, so let us stretch it usefully:

- The **menu** is the API documentation — the list of everything available.
- Each **dish** is an *endpoint*: a specific URL representing a specific thing, like `https://api.github.com/users/torvalds`.
- **How you ask** is the *method*: are you ordering (creating), asking what is available (reading), changing your order (updating), or cancelling (deleting)?
- Your **table number and ID** are the *headers*, especially the authentication token that proves you are allowed to order.
- **"No onions, extra spicy"** are the *parameters* and *request body* — the details of what exactly you want.
- The **waiter's reply** is the *response*, and their tone — "here you go" vs "we're out of that" vs "the kitchen is on fire" — is the *status code*.

Where the analogy breaks: unlike a waiter, an API is completely literal. Mistype one character in a field name and you get an error, not a helpful clarification. Precision is the whole job.

##### HTTP methods: the four verbs

APIs on the web run on HTTP, the same protocol your browser uses. HTTP defines **methods** — verbs describing your intent.

| Method | Intent | Example | Changes data? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `GET` | Read something | Fetch a user's profile | No |
| `POST` | Create something new | Add a new contact | Yes |
| `PUT` / `PATCH` | Update existing | Change a contact's phone | Yes |
| `DELETE` | Remove something | Delete a record | Yes |

The distinction between `PUT` and `PATCH` is worth knowing: `PUT` replaces the *whole* record (any field you leave out may be wiped), while `PATCH` updates only the fields you send. When an automation mysteriously blanks out half a customer record, a `PUT` where a `PATCH` was needed is usually the culprit.

`GET` is called *safe* because it should never change anything. This is why you can retry a failed `GET` freely, but retrying a failed `POST` might create two orders — a real problem you will meet in the error-handling module.

##### Anatomy of a request

A request has four parts. Here is a complete one, written in the universal command-line tool `curl`:

```bash
curl -X POST "https://api.example.com/v1/contacts?source=website" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_live_EXAMPLE_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
        "name": "Ananya Rao",
        "email": "ananya@example.com",
        "tags": ["lead", "webinar"]
      }'
```

Reading it piece by piece:

- **Method and URL** — `POST` to the `/v1/contacts` endpoint.
- **Query parameters** — `?source=website`. These ride in the URL after `?`, joined by `&`, and are typically used for filtering, searching, sorting, and pagination: `?page=2&per_page=50&status=active`.
- **Headers** — metadata about the request. `Authorization` carries your credential (here a bearer token). `Content-Type: application/json` tells the server how to interpret the body. `Accept` tells it what format you want back.
- **Body** — the actual data being sent, as JSON. Only used with `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`.

A rule that catches everyone once: **`GET` requests do not have a body.** If you need to send filters with a `GET`, they go in query parameters.

##### Responses and status codes

The server replies with a status code, headers, and usually a JSON body.

```json
{
  "id": "cnt_88213",
  "name": "Ananya Rao",
  "email": "ananya@example.com",
  "created_at": "2026-03-14T09:12:44Z"
}
```

Status codes are grouped by their first digit, and memorizing the groups is more useful than memorizing individual codes:

- **2xx — success.** `200 OK` (here it is), `201 Created` (new thing made), `204 No Content` (worked, nothing to return — common for `DELETE`).
- **3xx — redirection.** `301`/`302`: the resource moved. Usually handled for you.
- **4xx — you made a mistake.** `400 Bad Request` (malformed body), `401 Unauthorized` (missing or invalid credentials), `403 Forbidden` (valid credentials, insufficient permission), `404 Not Found` (wrong URL or the record does not exist), `422 Unprocessable Entity` (valid JSON but failed validation), `429 Too Many Requests` (rate limited — slow down).
- **5xx — the server made a mistake.** `500 Internal Server Error`, `502 Bad Gateway`, `503 Service Unavailable`.

The practical significance: **4xx means fix your request; 5xx means retry later.** That single sentence drives how you configure error handling in every automation you will ever build. Note the difference between `401` and `403` too — one means "who are you?", the other means "I know who you are, and no."

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Z as Automation Platform
    participant A as App API
    Z->>A: POST /v1/contacts + headers + JSON body
    A->>A: authenticate, validate, save
    A-->>Z: 201 Created + {"id": "cnt_88213"}
    Z->>A: GET /v1/contacts/cnt_88213
    A-->>Z: 200 OK + full contact JSON
    Z->>A: POST /v1/contacts (bad token)
    A-->>Z: 401 Unauthorized + {"error": "invalid_token"}
```

##### How to read API documentation

Documentation looks intimidating until you know that you only need five things from any endpoint's page:

1. **Base URL** — e.g. `https://api.github.com`. Note the version (`/v1/`, `/v3/`).
2. **Authentication** — API key in a header? Bearer token? OAuth? This section is usually called "Authentication" or "Getting started" and you should read it first.
3. **The endpoint and method** — `POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues`. Curly braces mean *substitute your value here*.
4. **Parameters** — a table of names, types, and whether each is required. Required fields are where 400 errors come from.
5. **Example request and response** — copy this, change one thing at a time.

Also skim the **rate limits** section (how many requests per minute you are allowed) and **pagination** (how to get results 51–100). GitHub's API docs are an excellent model; try `https://api.github.com/users/torvalds` in a browser right now — it is a public `GET` with no authentication and returns clean JSON immediately.

##### Common pitfalls

- **Forgetting `Content-Type: application/json`.** The server receives your body as plain text and rejects it with a confusing 400.
- **Sending an API key in query parameters.** Query strings appear in server logs and browser history. Use headers.
- **Ignoring pagination.** Your automation processes 100 records and silently misses 4,900 more.
- **Trailing slashes and http vs https.** `http://` often redirects, and some tools drop the body during a redirect. Always use the exact URL from the docs.
- **Testing against production.** Use the sandbox/test credentials that most serious APIs provide. Creating 40 test invoices in a live accounting system is a memorable way to learn this.
- **Assuming an error means "nothing happened."** A `504 Gateway Timeout` sometimes means the action *did* succeed and the response was lost.

##### Your hands-on tie-in

Today's practical task: make a `GET` request to `https://api.github.com/users/torvalds` using Postman or your browser, and explicitly identify three things — the **status code**, at least two **response headers** (look for `x-ratelimit-remaining`, it tells you how many calls you have left), and the **JSON body**. Seeing that rate-limit header early is a small revelation about how APIs really work.

Then take the mini project further: pick GitHub, OpenWeather, or JSONPlaceholder, read the docs properly, and make one `GET` and one `POST`-style request, documenting the endpoint, method, parameters and response. JSONPlaceholder accepts fake `POST`s, which makes it perfect for safe practice. Finish with your **cheat-sheet** of the four methods and five status codes in plain language — you will genuinely refer back to it.

##### Key takeaways

- An API is a documented contract for how software asks other software to do things; every automation platform is an API client underneath.
- `GET` reads, `POST` creates, `PUT`/`PATCH` update, `DELETE` removes — and only `GET` is safe to retry blindly.
- A request is method + URL + query parameters + headers (auth, content type) + body; a response is status code + headers + body.
- 2xx succeeded, 4xx is your fault (fix the request), 5xx is theirs (retry later). This rule drives all error handling.
- Reading docs is a five-item checklist: base URL, auth, endpoint/method, parameters, example — plus rate limits and pagination.
